catalog_quote: However, the quantity of a vowel occurring in mono-syllabic words, close or open, depends much on the accent on it, ie. the quantity of the vowel is shorter if there is a stress accent and longer if a pitch accent which in some cases is significant as well. (see 1.2.2.b) e.g. it is short in /ips/ sleep, /rin/ sister, /kum/ pillow, /sar/ ear-ring, /go/ rock, /ro/ corpse, /cher/ anxious, due to prominent stress accent on them but it is comparatively long in /ga/ wound, /cha/ tooth, /fia/ nose, /pi/ four, /de/ horn, /di/ this, /du/ that; /mi/ man, /roz/ daily. Incidently, most of the words with short quantity are in close syliables and with long quantity in open syllables, though the underlying force is accent itself. ... (b) Accent: Accent is a phonemic feature in Tinani. The examples of its phonemic contrast may be illustrated as below: /l4/ moon : /la/ goat /la’n/ air : /lén/ reply. ...…

(2) The classification 'tonal / tonal-OR-pitch accent, no positional stress rule' rests on D. D. Sharma's 1989 grammar sketch, which is the same work as Glottolog's best-ranked description (Sharma 1992, pp. 111-186); nothing better is listed in Glottolog and nothing better surfaced from the sources I could reach. sources.citation: Singh, Jag Deva. 1989. Lahauli verb inflection. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 12(2): 41-49.
sources.quote: The phoneme chart closes with three suprasegmentals: 'level tone', 'falling tone', 'rising tone'; later the illustrative root is described as 'monomorphemic and CVC type with a rising tone'. Nothing on word stress. Caveat: Singh calls the language only 'Lahauli' (Glottolog files it under tina1246; pronoun ge 'I' is shared by Tinan and Manchad, so dialect identity is not provable from the paper).
sources.locator: p.41, sec. 2 'The sound system of this Lahauli dialect' (variety of Nalda village, P.O. Muring, Tahsil Keylong); p.48 sec. 17(i)

sources.quote: None for Tinani. The volume's 'Lahauli' is explicitly 'also known as Stod-Bhoti ... Tibetic', data from Udaipur tehsil and Kullu, i.e. a different languoid; 'Tinani/Rangloyi' appears only as a name in a list of Himachal mother tongues.
